Clean energy solutions at the household level
Air pollution and health training toolkit for health workers (APHT)
World Health Organization (WHO) reference number for the module Clean energy solutions at the household level is WHO/PPC/ECO/CAE/2026.1 © WHO 2026. Some rights reserved. This work is available under the CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO licence.
This module contains a large set of slides from which the presenter should select the most relevant ones to use for a specific presentation. These slides cover many facets of the issue. You can present only those slides that apply most directly to the local or regional situation. Where relevant, you can adapt the information, statistics and photos within each slide to the particular context in which this module is being presented.
This module belongs to the Air Pollution and Health Training (APHT) toolkit targeting health workers. It has been developed in collaboration with more than 30 experts from government agencies, WHO collaborating centres, and non-state actors, including medical and environmental health associations, as well as academic institutions. The methodology used for development included a mapping exercise of existing air pollution and health training opportunities targeting health workers, which informed gaps and needs for a global set of materials. Experts identified through existing collaborations with WHO contributed to defining the outline and populating the training modules with content. Peer review and pilot testing in the field coordinated by WHO ensured the collection of feedback and input for the finalization of the products. WHO made all possible efforts to ensure geographical and gender balance for developing this training toolkit, acknowledging limitations regarding expertise, experience and overall feasibility.
The APHT toolkit to which this module belongs is a comprehensive set of materials exploring different air pollution and health topics. Developed under a global perspective, it can serve different types of audiences within the health sectors while taking into account the variety of roles within the public health workforce. The toolkit aims to provide health workers with the knowledge and tools necessary to understand and address the health effects of air pollution and mitigate risks by effectively engaging with patients, individuals and communities, while advocating for clean air interventions. The toolkit was built around the concept of train-the trainer, which means trainees are enabled to become trainers and educate peers and communities. Pilot tested in different fora and settings including in-person WHO workshops held in Ghana in 2022 and in Rwanda in 2024 in collaboration with the related Ministries of Health, this toolkit allows participants to engage in comprehensive, distributive learning of knowledge and skills, enabling them to effectively train others. Key health professionals were invited to join a series of events to pilot the training materials and actively contribute to the finalization of the toolkit elements. You can use and have access to other APHT modules where relevant. To see the full package visit: https://www.who.int/tools/air-pollution-and-health-training-toolkit-for-health-workers
The APHT pilot workshop held in Ghana in 2022 produced a published report. The workshop report serves as a tool and example of a training that can be replicated and adapted to other contexts and settings based on country and regional priorities and needs. To learn more about the pilot exercise and lessons learned, please review the full report here: Building health workforce capacity on air pollution and health
WHO engaged experts from academic institutions for external peer review, including through WHO Collaborating Centres. WHO proposed the module outline, which was refined by the main contributors through group and targeted discussions. One author drafted the content and ensured its accuracy and completeness, with expert input. The draft training module underwent multiple rounds of review by WHO and independent external reviewers from different regions. All external experts submitted to WHO a declaration of interest disclosing potential conflicts of interest that might affect, or might reasonably be perceived to affect, their objectivity and independence in relation to the subject matter of this guidance. WHO reviewed each of the declarations and concluded that none could give rise to a potential or reasonably perceived conflict of interest related to the subjects discussed at the meeting or covered by the guidance
The case studies presented in this module are mainly derived from the WHO Household Energy Assessment Rapid Tools (HEART) reports. They were selected based on geographical representation and the relevance of the proposed interventions, while also aiming to differentiate the interventions presented in the module to provide examples of various energy transitions to clean or cleaner fuel and device combinations. In addition, an internal consultation was conducted with advisers in the Pan American Health Organization to provide a regional perspective that was not covered by the WHO HEART reports at the time of the module’s development. For more information: https://www.who.int/tools/household-energy-assessment-rapid-tool-templates

## Definition: household air pollution (HAP)
A type of indoor air pollution generated by inefficient household fuel combustion leading to air pollution indoors and outdoors.
Released from incomplete combustion of polluting fuels (i.e. wood, dung, charcoal, coal, kerosene).
<drawing id="im-43a95bd10ce7a1c392e48c276a194cc5-0011" format="jpg" path="air-38_WHO_Fact sheet 附件_Clean household energy solutions (清洁家用能源)_2024.blocks.assets/4f0b30569c3f53d057d978ebaecf6122d497dd7f14bfd317df4f24072332d710.jpg" src="" />
Caused when polluting fuels are used in combination with inefficient technologies.
• Commonly released as a result of cooking, heating and lighting.
<drawing id="im-43a95bd10ce7a1c392e48c276a194cc5-0012" format="jpg" path="air-38_WHO_Fact sheet 附件_Clean household energy solutions (清洁家用能源)_2024.blocks.assets/fe85ebe72b61f27b562f2d31d56ea0ec9774ff4beae387cf8367e1a9c1d26422.jpg" src="" />

• Refers to pollution in and around the home (not just indoors!).
<drawing id="im-43a95bd10ce7a1c392e48c276a194cc5-0016" format="jpg" path="air-38_WHO_Fact sheet 附件_Clean household energy solutions (清洁家用能源)_2024.blocks.assets/472cb3522a30ae8a40e37acd5e0d94f8dfec92b7640b44fc6cad97cad7928cdd.jpg" src="" />
You may now be quite familiar with the definition of household air pollution as “air pollution generated by household fuel combustion, that causes both indoor air pollution and contributes to ambient air pollution”.
Household air pollution (HAP) is air pollution released from incomplete combustion of polluting fuels (i.e. wood, dung, charcoal, coal, kerosene). It is indeed generated by the inefficient use of fuels and technologies for domestic activities such as cooking, heating and lighting.
Household air pollution is a type of indoor air pollution and contributes to outdoor air pollution.
When we refer to HAP, we are considering the mixture of pollutants released as a result of the incomplete combustion (remember this!) of carbon-based fuels (solid fuels, kerosene), not only indoors but in and around the home. These fuels are used for household activities such as cooking, heating and lighting.
For the sake of completeness, we should call it “household air pollution from the use of inefficient fuel and technologies”, where the expression “fuel and technologies” encompasses different types of both fuels (solid and liquid) and polluting devices (stoves, lamps, etc.) used for cooking, heating and lighting.

# Proportion of population with access to clean cooking fuels and technologies (%), 2024
<drawing id="im-43a95bd10ce7a1c392e48c276a194cc5-0019" format="jpg" path="air-38_WHO_Fact sheet 附件_Clean household energy solutions (清洁家用能源)_2024.blocks.assets/11f5d4bde87ee91d822fa8f59740003888720ea6a73032acf34a6ad35b5c3ed5.jpg" src="" />
When you look at the graph on the previous slide (deaths attributable to household air pollution) and the percentage of the population with access to clean household energy on the map) it is clear that the disease burden closely mirrors the prevalence of polluting fuel use for cooking (a proxy indicator for household air pollution exposure).
Recognizing this tremendous disease burden and the challenges faced by countries to tackle it, WHO released the first set of health-based normative guidance on household air pollution in 2014 (WHO Guidelines for indoor air quality: household fuel combustion). Much of the information contained in this module is based on these guidelines. These guidelines provide evidence-based recommendations on the technical and policy aspects related to the transition to fuels and technology combinations that are clean for health.
Note: To estimate the number of deaths attributable to household air pollution, the population attributable fraction calculation is used based on the number of people exposed to household air pollution, the disease risk level associated with different levels of $\mathsf { P M } _ { 2 . 5 }$ exposure for men, women and children, and the underlying disease rate in the given population.

Around 25% of the world’s population, mainly in LMICs, cooks with fuels and polluting stoves that emit substantial amounts of toxic and health-damaging air pollutants. This poses a great risk to human health.
The percentage of the population exposed to household air pollution varies across different regions of the world. Much of Asia and many Latin American countries have made substantial progress in reducing exposure to household air pollution over the last decade or so. However, in the African Region, the population exposed to household ai pollution is growing annually, as the growth in access to clean cooking technologies is slower than the population growth in the region over the same period. In sub-Saharan Africa, the number of people without access is still increasing by about 14 million people each year, as population growth outpaces gains in access.

The "environmental health pathway" of household energy use to health impacts clarifies the sources of ill health caused by household energy use and, more importantly, the opportunities to "intervene" to reduce exposure and protect health.
The combustion (burning) process is key to understanding the main health risks for household energy use. In an ideal situation, complete or efficient combustion would result only in water and carbon dioxide (CO ), both with little to no impact on health
However, when there is not enough oxygen to allow the fuel to burn or "combust" completely, other byproducts are produced (e.g. carbon monoxide [CO], particulate matter [PM]), many of which are damaging to health. These by byproducts are commonly referred to as “products of incomplete combustion” or PICs. There are hundreds of PICs resulting from the inefficient combustion of some household fuels that are released into the immediate environment, often referred to together as “household air pollution”.
The traditional and simple stoves and devices commonly used in households in LMICs are very inefficient; meaning when fuels are burned in them, they produce a lot of PICs, often in high concentrations. In contrast, cleaner options, like electricity, gaseous (e.g. LPG) or liquid (e.g. ethanol) fuels burn very efficiently producing low levels of emissions, or in the case of electricity, none at all, at point of use.
Hence, by replacing the more polluting traditional or simple stoves with ones that are more efficient, e.g. “cleaner burning”, the intervention is addressing the sources of emissions to reduce health risk.
Replacing the source of emission with cleaner fuels or electricity may not always be feasible in the near term, and in these cases, in the interim, one can look elsewhere on the environmental pathway for other interventions to reduce health risk. For example, interventions to reduce the “concentrations” of HAP in the household will reduce levels of HAP exposure, and lower health risk. In these cases, some types of improved solid fuel stoves (i.e. advanced combustion stoves) that are more efficient can be promoted in the transition to much cleaner options, as their use will lead to less fuel use, fewer emissions of PICs, and hence lower exposure and health risk.
Note: It is important to note, to ensure any lower risk in health, emissions need to be significantly lower than what is typically measured with biomass stoves.
Other interventions on the environmental health pathway focus on reducing the personal level of exposure to HAP. For example, if a home is ventilated (e.g. windows in kitchen), or the stove has a chimney or flue, some of the emissions escape to the outside resulting in a lower concentration of pollution in the home and consequently reduced exposure to individuals indoors.
The air quality in and around the home is most important, but another key factor is the duration of time that a person stays in the polluted environment. Basic guidance to minimize time exposed to high levels of HAP by moving to less polluted areas also serves as a simple intervention that can help prevent disease.
Note: It is important to remember that PICs emissions do not just disappear; rather they are sent outdoors and ultimately increase local ambient air pollution, affecting others in the neighbouring community or even circulating back into the house from which they came.

content:
## Climate impacts
Polluting fuels and technologies contribute to global warming as they emit both CO and SLCPs.
<drawing id="im-43a95bd10ce7a1c392e48c276a194cc5-0025" format="jpg" path="air-38_WHO_Fact sheet 附件_Clean household energy solutions (清洁家用能源)_2024.blocks.assets/be0961ea3116553bf9a3a53047a06418c6214ee2caa294ea59b06eebf2d0619f.jpg" src="" />
Household energy use has other impacts beyond disease-specific outcomes.
Safety risks: burns and poisoning. The use of traditional stoves and kerosene lamps presents serious safety risks, especially to those using them and to young children. For example, cooking on the floor can result in children being burned or the cook’s clothes catching fire, while unstable pots may lead to scalding from spillage of hot liquids. Kerosene stoves and lamps are a common cause of fires, and storing kerosene fuel in soft drinks or water bottles results in many cases of childhood poisonings, as when the fuel is mistaken and ingested.
Gender: the procurement and/or use of fuels in the household is very time consuming. Mostly women and children are tasked with fuel collection and stove preparation. These activities can be time consuming, taking hours of useful time away from schooling, income generation, leisure or other activities. Other associated health risks with fuel collection include violence, particularly for woman and girls, as well as injury from snake and animal bites or musculoskeletal from the weight of the fuel carried.
Energy supply and deforestation: the use of household energy must start with obtaining the fuel, whether this be the collection of wood and other “free” biomass fuel or the supply and purchase of fuels like charcoal, gas or electricity.
The collection of wood fuel and the production of charcoal can significantly impact the local environment, especially where forest resources are not sustainably managed. Loss of forest cover can contribute to soil erosion and flooding.
Climate impacts: emissions from the incomplete combustion of solid household fuels and kerosene, including products of incomplete combustion (PICs), such as methane and black carbon, have very powerful short-term warming effects on the climate, the so-called short-lived climate pollutants (SLCPs). Longer term warming effects occur mainly with ${ \mathsf { C O } } _ { 2 }$ emissions. Biomass fuels such as wood, if fully renewably harvested, can, in theory at least, be climate neutral in terms of ${ \mathsf { C O } } _ { 2 }$ emissions. However, estimates suggest around 30% of the wood fuel harvested globally is unsustainable, resulting in climate-damaging emissions equivalent to around 2% of global emissions. In addition, as the combustion process with solid biomass fuel is typically very incomplete (even with “improved” solid fuel stoves), the overall effect on the climate includes warming from both PICs (short-term) and CO (longer term) emissions.
Cleaner burning fuels also have impacts on the environment and climate. For example, although LPG burns very efficiently with minimal emissions of PICs and does not impact on forest reserves, it is a fossil fuel so it inevitably makes a contribution to atmospheric ${ \mathsf { C O } } _ { 2 } .$ The chemical composition of LPG (with a relatively large hydrogen to carbon ratio), however, means that for the energy delivered, it contributes far less ${ \mathsf { C O } } _ { 2 }$ than other fossil fuels such as coal.
We will return to the climate and health benefit of LPG and other clean fuels later in this presentation.

# Importance of clean cooking for achieving SDG 7 and SDG 3
<drawing id="im-43a95bd10ce7a1c392e48c276a194cc5-0027" format="jpg" path="air-38_WHO_Fact sheet 附件_Clean household energy solutions (清洁家用能源)_2024.blocks.assets/260c0762019f66d53c4e2b7639b04a8972c57344321f7491ac91d67d21b00e02.jpg" src="" />
Clean cooking is integral to the achievement of SDG 7 and to the sustainable development agenda more broadly: good health, well-being, gender equity, climate change and eliminating poverty.
Despite progress on other SDG 7 goals, clean household energy is still lagging behind. Urgent action is needed to accelerate progress through policy, financing and technology development.
<drawing id="im-43a95bd10ce7a1c392e48c276a194cc5-0028" format="jpg" path="air-38_WHO_Fact sheet 附件_Clean household energy solutions (清洁家用能源)_2024.blocks.assets/eb9b60b7c93a6605d79d839d9ac61c8a2ead48366862dbf543d27fa78410cd35.jpg" src="" />
In the next couple of slides, we will consider household energy related to cooking and its relevance to the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development.
The 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, adopted by all United Nations Member States in 2015, provides a shared blueprint for peace and prosperity for people and the planet, now and into the future. It includes 17 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), which are an urgent call for action by all countries – developed and developing – in a global partnership. The SDGs recognize that ending poverty and other deprivations must go handin-hand with strategies that improve health and education, reduce inequality and spur economic growth – all while tackling climate change and working to preserve our oceans and forests.
Several of the SDGs relate to clean household energy and health. For example, SDG 7 on energy is a commitment by countries to ensure access to affordable, reliable, sustainable and modern energy for all. One of the targets for SDG 7 is focused on ensuring universal access to clean cooking where “clean” is defined by the normative recommendations included in the WHO Guidelines for indoor air quality: household fuel combustion.
SDG 3, the SDG for health, includes a target to substantially reduce the number of deaths and illnesses from hazardous chemicals and air, water, and soil pollution and contamination. To track progress on this target, reductions in the mortality rate from the effects of exposure to ambient and household air pollution are monitored.
In summary, the integration of clean cooking into several SDGs has been an important mechanism to raise awareness and initiate urgent action and investment in accelerating the transition to clean cooking.

The development of global guidelines ensuring the appropriate use of evidence represents one of the core functions of WHO Normative recommendations that can impact upon health policies or clinical interventions are considered guidelines for WHO purposes. Topics for which WHO guidelines have been developed include antimicrobial resistance, child health, communicable and noncommunicable diseases, mental health and substance abuse, nutrition, public health emergencies, and many others.
In 1987, WHO produced the first evidence-based guidelines for air quality, setting recommended limits for health-harmfu concentrations of key air pollutants based on a global synthesis of scientific evidence. WHO global air quality guidelines cover annual and daily concentrations of fine particulates, nitrogen dioxide, sulfur dioxide, ozone and carbon monoxide (WHO, 2021). Other related guidelines for indoor air quality cover selected pollutants, including carbon monoxide (WHO, 2010). Relevant for this training module are the WHO guidelines for indoor air quality: household fuel combustion, which set limits on emissions from cooking and heating stoves and lighting devices, as well as recommendations on different fuels used in the home and policies for scaling up access to clean energy to maximize health benefits (WHO, 2014).
The latter are presented in this slide.
The WHO guidelines include four recommendations targeting national governments, agencies, providers, public and private energy production and supply utilities, health authorities and practitioners, NGOs and researchers. The recommendations focus on the reduction of emissions to protect health through the provision of emission rate targets that stove and devices should achieve. They also advise on the reduction of specific polluting fuels use, as well as the importance of maximizing health benefits in the transition to clean household energy use.
In brief, the guidelines recommend:
• Achieving emission targets for $\mathsf { P M } _ { 2 . 5 }$ and CO fuel and device combinations in order to protect health.
• Addressing all household energy end uses (cooking, heating, lighting).
● Prioritizing the cleanest stoves and fuels in the transition to clean household energy, acknowledging that in many countries, that transition to options that are truly “clean for health” will take time.
• Discontinuing the use of unprocessed coal as a household fuel, in light of the specific health risks.
• Discouraging the use of kerosene as a household fuel in light of concerns about emissions and safety.
The WHO household fuel combustion guidelines include interim emissions rate targets for $\mathsf { P M } _ { 2 . 5 }$ and CO that reflect the reality that, in some low-income households, baseline levels of pollution are very high, and meeting the guideline recommendations in the near term might not be feasible. In settings where the infrastructure for distributing LPG and supplying electricity is not yet in place – especially rural areas that lie well beyond existing supply chains and grid networks – people will continue to burn the fuel they can most easily access and afford
The guidelines also include a good practice recommendation on developing and implementing policy on climate change mitigation that considers co-benefits from health due to clean household energy use.

# Defining clean, transitional and polluting fuels and technologies
Clean fuels and technologies are those that meet WHO health-based emission targets for $\mathsf { P M } _ { 2 . 5 }$ and CO at the point of use, thereby minimizing household air pollution exposure. Emission targets are provided in the WHO guidelines for indoor air quality: household fuel consumption, which are linked to the WHO global air quality guidelines (AQG).
<drawing id="im-43a95bd10ce7a1c392e48c276a194cc5-0037" format="jpg" path="air-38_WHO_Fact sheet 附件_Clean household energy solutions (清洁家用能源)_2024.blocks.assets/aa07368b66eb2b5ced20da8dfcc1ec96b15a12954bb1d22368d06cf335f33fe2.jpg" src="" />
It is important to have a clear understanding of what is meant by “clean” energy for health. This is important for global monitoring of the access to and use of clean fuels and technologies around the world. Clean fuels and technologies are those that meet WHO health-based emission targets for $\mathsf { P M } _ { 2 . 5 }$ and CO at the point of use, thereby minimizing household air pollution exposure
The WHO guidelines provide device and fuel emission rates that are required to meet the levels of safety for $\mathsf { P M } _ { 2 . 5 }$ and CO for health.
We will go into detail on the clean fuel and technology options shortly, but in brief, currently, for global reporting purposes, WHO considers biogas, LPG, natural gas, electricity, ethanol and other alcohol fuels, and solar, to be clean for health at the point of use. This applies to cooking, heating and lighting.
Similarly, WHO considers that polluting fuels and technologies include open fires, kerosene, dung, candles and raw coal.
Kerosene and coal are always polluting and discouraged in the WHO guidelines. But what about biomass?

## Is biomass always polluting?
It depends on the type of biomass and the device it is used in – the determination of whether biomass is clean or polluting is made on an individual basis.
The device being used has a great impact on whether the cooking system is clean since it is the emissions resulting from the combination of fuel and device that determines whether the system is clean or not.
Therefore, wood, crop waste, dung, pellets and charcoal can be polluting or clean depending on the efficiency of the device that is being used for burning with that specific fuel. The more inefficient the fuel is burned; the more smoke is generated and emitted.
Processed biomass, like pellets, is a promising renewable fuel that can usually burn more cleanly than other biomass options.

When properly used and maintained, liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) and piped natural gas (PNG) stoves also produce low levels of emissions of $\mathsf { P M } _ { 2 . 5 }$ and CO and other products of incomplete combustion (PICs). Availability and affordability of these fuels still remain a challenge for more remote areas.
Stoves that use alcohol and ethanol fuels are also clean for health. Ethanol cooking devices are now available using an easy-to-use gel. Alcohol fuels are still limited but growing in availability.
Biogas is a promising alternative that burns as cleanly as LPG and PNG and, as a renewable fuel, has no negative climate impacts. Household biogas systems turn organic material from livestock manure, human waste or crop residues into methane and other combustible gases through anaerobic digestion. This gas is then piped into the house and can be used for cooking, lighting or powering an electric generator. However, biogas has some disadvantages: it requires sustained maintenance and a reliable supply of waste and water, which is not possible for all households. This also involves exposure to excrement that must be handled carefully to avoid infection of handlers.
Solar cooking devices – including panels, boxes and parabolic cookers – directly convert the sun’s energy into useful heat. They produce no harmful emissions and cost nothing to operate, but they tend to require longer cooking times, require greater adjustment in user behaviour, and they can only be used during times and seasons when there is adequate sunshine. Hence, they can be an appropriate, clean complement to a household cooking system but not always as the only solution
Biomass-burning stoves that meet WHO guideline levels are still not widely available, and those that have very low emissions are currently extremely expensive, with recurring fuel costs. New forced-draft biomass stoves offer the potential for meaningful fuel savings – an important consideration for many household cooks – as well as reductions in pollution exposures relative to traditional stoves or open fires. Currently, emissions from these stoves are not as clean as those from LPG or electric cooking but can serve as an important transitional cleaner stove, particularly in more remote settings where infrastructure is limited. Further innovation, research and investment are indeed to produce affordable biomass stoves that meet the WHO guidelines.

## Switching from polluting to clean: examples
From coal to electricity
From wood to electricity
From kerosene lamp to battery-powered torch
Addressing all the sources of household air pollution is critical to protecting health.
Here are three example of switching from polluting to clean energy:
• To achieve clean cooking, households could switch from burning coal to electricity.
• Rather than space heating with an open fire, households could use an electric space heater.
• A clean lighting system could be a battery-powered torch or flashlight instead of a kerosene lamp.
We give these examples as a reminder that it is not enough to only achieve clean cooking, but it is important for all energy uses in the home to be clean in order to protect health. If the household switches to an LPG stove but still heats with an open fire, most of the benefit of the clean stove is eliminated.
It is also important to ensure ALL household energy fuels and devices are clean to protect health. For example, just mainly using LPG for cooking, but supplementing that cookstove with an open fire or simple biomass stove will also negate many if not all health benefits.
Given the diversity of household energy practices and preferences across cultural and economic contexts, there is no one-size-fits-all answer. All of the clean solutions – LPG, PNG, electricity, biogas, solar energy and more efficient biomass devices – have roles to play in the effort to achieve universal access to clean household energy by 2030.

# Fuel stacking = parallel use of multiple types of fuel and technologies in a single household
<drawing id="im-43a95bd10ce7a1c392e48c276a194cc5-0054" format="jpg" path="air-38_WHO_Fact sheet 附件_Clean household energy solutions (清洁家用能源)_2024.blocks.assets/c17ebc8e9b30c1bb3d939bf5e45fcadc96abd7becfac47d96cdb5b42ee4fd393.jpg" src="" />
Fuel and stove stacking is the parallel use of multiple types of fuel and technologies in a single household and often at the same time
Even after gaining access to a clean energy option such as LPG, members of a household might continue to cook or heat their home with an open fire or with a traditional wood-burning stove. Or they may continue to use kerosene lamps in certain rooms to supplement electric lights, even after being connected to the grid.
There are many reasons why people stack fuels and devices. A given stove may have some benefits for the user – convenience, reliability, affordability – but still not meet all of the user’s preferences. For instance, a cook may decide to continue using an inefficient older stove because their pots do not fit on a new “improved” one. A family that cooks with gas may keep a solid fuel stove in operation as a backup in case the supply of LPG is disrupted. In some colder areas, traditional stoves may be kept in use for heating, even though LPG is used for cooking. In many places, such as in parts of rural China, people may cook their own meals with gas or electricity but still use open fires and simple stoves to prepare feed for their animals.
Stacking is almost inevitable as households start to transition to cleaner and more efficient stoves and fuels. While it is not the ideal situation in terms of reducing HAP as much as possible, it does signify that new technologies and fuels are being used to some extent. The goal should be to encourage households to use the cleanest options as much as possible, and ultimately – when cost, availability, cultural or other barriers that hold them back have been overcome – exclusively.

<drawing id="im-43a95bd10ce7a1c392e48c276a194cc5-0076" format="jpg" path="air-38_WHO_Fact sheet 附件_Clean household energy solutions (清洁家用能源)_2024.blocks.assets/ede6c039d3fe6b969315450b631c36e146e221e8c9693c6ca3e82d94bad81181.jpg" src="" />
Barriers to the adoption of cleaner fuels and technology solutions need to be taken into consideration to obtain the whole picture about energy access and use.
We will mainly focus on fuels and stoves for cooking purposes as this is the most universal source of household air pollution.
These barriers can be grouped into three main categories:
• sociocultural context
• economic barriers
• other factors hindering the switch to clean cooking stoves and fuels.
Let’s describe each of them further.
heading: Barriers to adopting cleaner fuels and technology solutions

## • Level of education:
people with lower education tend to be more reluctant to change.
<drawing id="im-43a95bd10ce7a1c392e48c276a194cc5-0078" format="jpg" path="air-38_WHO_Fact sheet 附件_Clean household energy solutions (清洁家用能源)_2024.blocks.assets/7a44e5afa83d1acc4a3c6ceb5f63350b25f8d39567305b54021c9c07f949c757.jpg" src="" />
Sociocultural barriers to clean cooking include:
• Cultural beliefs and preferences, such as a concern that certain foods taste best using traditional cooking may prevent change to a clean fuel such as LPG.
• Gender norms, such as who is in charge in the house of cooking practices, who has decision-making power or control over household finances.
• Large household size requires more energy but may mean there is more labour available to collect firewood (less incentive to change).
• Community interactions, e.g. where poor experiences with a particular stove are passed on, may contribute to community-wide resistance to change. The opposite may apply to good experiences.
• Lower education level is associated with greater reluctance to change; the time of less-educated women may also be less valued.

## Economic
• Income level or irregular income may be insufficient for purchasing.
• Prioritization, e.g. school fees, health care and other expenditures are seen as more important.
Perceived affordability, if fuel is purchased in small quantities, larger quantity outlay (e.g. LPG cylinder) may be perceived as unaffordable.
• Upfront investment not always possible.
Lack of regulation and standardization.
<drawing id="im-43a95bd10ce7a1c392e48c276a194cc5-0080" format="jpg" path="air-38_WHO_Fact sheet 附件_Clean household energy solutions (清洁家用能源)_2024.blocks.assets/7a18f11d92db486fc05653943492026f920ccf71817848fb4d6d059b8ffbb759.jpg" src="" />
Economic barriers to the adoption of cleaner fuels include:
• Income level may be insufficient to purchase stoves and cover ongoing fuel costs.
• Other priorities for household expenditure, such as school fees, health care, etc. may compete and be seen as more important.
If households habitually collect or purchase fuel in small quantities (e.g. charcoal, kerosene), the large upfront investment for a 12.5 kg LPG cylinder refill, for example, is perceived as unaffordable even though, in fact, the household may spend more combined on all the small quantities of fuels like charcoal.
• Irregular or seasonal income variations may further undermine the ability to cover the upfront investment and fuel costs.
At a national scale, economic barriers include a lack of regulation and standardization, insufficient monetary and fiscal policies, lack of prioritization and allocated resources, and poor cross-sectoral coordination.

Safety perceptions (e.g. LPG and explosions).
Unavailability or only intermittent availability.
Stove performance in terms of low emissions and fuel savings do not meet users' expectations.
Lack of “cleaner” transitional solutions with some health benefits, particularly in more rural or remote areas.

## Other important factors include:
• Some devices might be perceived as unsafe; this applies in particular to LPG. National-level policies to ensure a safe and well-regulated market is critical.
• Some fuel and technologies might be unavailable or only available intermittently.
• Stove performance might not decrease emissions and save fuel as expected among users.
heading: Other important factors include:

content:
## Empowering women's access to clean energy
• Drive demand as consumers and users.
• Influence behaviour change through peer-to-peer communication.
<drawing id="im-43a95bd10ce7a1c392e48c276a194cc5-0083" format="jpg" path="air-38_WHO_Fact sheet 附件_Clean household energy solutions (清洁家用能源)_2024.blocks.assets/18258f125546c2164cee1bc37d25636505eeea618247cfe66979fb1a82221154.jpg" src="" />
• Better reach female consumers.
Engage in existing networks for the promotion of clean technologies use.
Case study from Kenya: empowering sales capacity of females in the energy sector A 2015 study showed that empowerment training in Kenya led to the sale of cookstoves more than doubling. Women sales representatives who received empowerment training outsold men by a margin of 3 to 1.
Women serve as not only the primary cooks and fuel procurers but also often take on household management responsibilities, spending substantial time at home. Their lives are significantly impacted by the choice of fuels and technologies for cooking, heating and lighting. Women can play a crucial role in the energy sector, acting as both consumers and users, influencing behavioural change within their communities, and participating in or establishing networks to promote the adoption of new technologies.
The introduction of clean cooking fuels can substantially reduce the time women spend on unpaid work associated with meal preparation, thanks to faster cooking times and diminished need for fuel collection trips. Clean fuels and technologies are also cost-efficient, resulting in long-term economic savings. The time and income saved can create more opportunities for activities that enhance the well-being of women and girls, contributing to lifting them out of energy poverty.
Various case studies have demonstrated that empowering women through participation in the energy value chain (e.g. selling stoves) can lead to a significant increase in sales. For instance, a 2015 study in Kenya revealed that empowerment training resulted in more than doubling the sales of cookstoves. Women sales representatives who underwent empowerment training outsold their male counterparts by a three-to-one margin.

CHEST is the Clean Household Energy Solutions Toolkit, a WHO resource that aims to give decision-makers and implementing partners the tools and resources to scale up clean and safe interventions in the home. CHEST provides tools for facilitating the design of policies that promote the adoption of clean household energy at a local, programme or national level.
As you can see on the slide, CHEST includes resources for conducting stakeholder mapping; accomplishing a needs assessment and situation analysis; identifying technological and policy intervention options; setting standards; performing monitoring and evaluation; engaging the health community; and improving communications and raising awareness.
Each topic is addressed within the Clean household energy policy and programme planning guide and accompanied by lessons learned from piloting, case studies or other experiences.
The toolkit is intended to help health sector professionals and policy-makers working in health or other sectors to plan and integrate the recommendations of the WHO Guidelines on indoor air quality: household fuel combustion into existing or future policies and programmes. It provides resources to guide the energy planning process, using evidence from WHO databases and training materials.
For more information: https://www.who.int/tools/clean-household-energy-solutions-toolkit

## Module 1
This module provides guidance on identifying key stakeholders and performing a country-wide assessment of household energy use. Since clean household energy solutions are multisectoral, it is critical that the appropriate stakeholders are included in decision-making. Equally important is understanding what technologies and fuels are used for cooking, heating and lighting, and the resulting air pollution exposures and health risks.
This module emphasizes the importance of considering the entire energy value chain (e.g. including supply), and the value of establishing a baseline to inform effective monitoring of the impacts from household energy policies and interventions. As part of this module, gaps in available data that must be addressed and the priority areas for policy development are identified. Application of the module tools will result in an evidence-based argument and potential paths forward for action on clean household energy.

## Module 2
This module provides resources for comparing various options for clean household energy interventions. The module and its associated tools help users explore how different fuels, technologies and policy designs can impact health, environmental and other social and economic outcomes, such as those related to livelihood and equity.
The module includes resources for identifying fuels and technologies that can be considered clean and safe, estimating the potential health and safety impacts, exploring the cost-effectiveness of different interventions and considering some of the key behavioural factors related to the sustained adoption of household energy (e.g. user satisfaction).
This module also emphasizes the importance of considering factors that contribute to an enabling policy environment for clean household energy interventions (i.e. successful plans, laws and policies), as well as the need to identify drivers and bottlenecks for implementation. WHO has developed a policy repository, which includes examples of household energy policies and programmes from countries around the world.

Internationally recognized standards for household energy devices serve an important role by providing clear information on device performance. Standards can give consumers confidence that the device will be reliable and achieve certain benefits (e.g. fuel savings and emissions reduction) and also help manufacturers ensure they meet regulatory requirements.
This module includes resources to help planners develop national standards for stoves based on safety, performance, durability and other features.

## Modules 5 and 6
The two final modules of CHEST provide health professionals with the tools to assess household energy as a risk factor for disease and to “prescribe” clean household energy solutions. It contains resources for the health sector to effectively communicate the health risks from household energy use, especially to those working in other sectors.
Here you can look at the audiences where health professionals can play a role.
First of all, regarding themselves and their peers, for example:
• Self education: if you are here it means you are empowering your own role as a health professional in the context of air pollution and health.
Organize education and training moments among your peers: you can re-use this material and adapt it to your needs. Sharing knowledge is essential!
Contribute to household air pollution and health scientific research: if you are part of a research group, consider including a household air pollution perspective!
Health professionals also can play a role in educating patients and the community, such as:
Raise awareness and promote behavioural change: you are an important advocate for switching to clean solutions at the individual/community level (e.g. you can fight cultural misbeliefs such as “my grandmother used a wood stove and she is fine, so smoke is not so harmful”).
• Encourage primary prevention actions: e.g. reduce emissions through clean household energy access.
And secondary prevention messages: e.g. reduce exposure through appropriate ventilation of the house, when this is possible – this is just an example.
And finally, health workers can collaborate with institutions:
• Collect data on patients’ exposure: use of screening tools – sharing data with ministries of health and local health authorities.
Advocate for funds dedicated to investigating the health effects of HAP as well as the health benefits of clean energy solutions interventions.
• Advocate for subsidization of clean energy solutions and introduction of monetary and fiscal policies to protect the most vulnerable from carrying the economic burden of transitioning from dirty to clean energy.

The Global Burn Registry provides a standardized platform for data collection, analysis and dissemination regarding burns. The registry is based on an easy-to-use data collection form designed by WHO and a network of global experts. The form is used for patients who are admitted to a health facility with burns. Data can be accessed and exported through the online Global Burn Registry interface maintained by WHO. The data collection form is available in English, French and Spanish.
Since most patients admitted for burns are in a health facility for days or weeks there is ample time to fill out the form and it does not interfere with the provision of emergency care. It takes approximately 5 minutes for clinical staff to complete the form – most of the form uses check boxes, so there is very little writing involved.
The Global Burn Registry was recently updated with a focus on household energy and includes questions about burns caused by cooking, heating and lighting, including the type of energy used, where the burn occurred, and information about the cooking area.

# Principles for protecting health against the harmful effects of household air pollution
• Reduce the time spent close to the pollution source (e.g. polluting cookstove).

Ensure better ventilation of the spaces through chimneys, windows and vents.
Explore possibilities of using cleaner fuels and technologies such as LPG and/or electricity.
“Prescribe” clean household energy solutions for your families and communities!
To mitigate the health risks from HAP, health workers can advise individuals and families to:
Minimize exposure to HAP by reducing the time spent close to the pollution source, especially vulnerable population groups (e.g. neonates/children, pregnant women, people older than 65 years and individuals with relevant comorbidities).
• Minimize concentrations of HAP within the home through better ventilation (e.g. chimneys, windows, vents, etc.).
• Minimize emissions from fuel combustion: control HAP at source (e.g. by burning fuels more efficiently or using cleaner fuels such as gas and/or electricity).
Reducing emissions involves keeping the home and fuel dry. Damp fuel emits more air pollutants than dry fuel when burned. Dampness in buildings is also associated with an increased risk of adverse respiratory outcomes. Reducing concentrations of emissions through ventilation lowers their accumulation indoors and therefore improves the qualit of indoor air. However, venting high concentrations of household air pollution will increase outdoor (also known as ambient) air pollution.

Household air pollution from cooking, heating and lighting is a major health issue, especially in LMICs. Children and women are most affected because they spend more time near indoor smoke.
To tackle this urgent public health problem, the WHO Collaborating Centre at the University of Liverpool and the Global Health Research Unit in the United Kingdom developed the CLEAN-Air(Africa) initiative in partnership with the Kenyan Ministry of Health. Together, they created the Community Household Air Pollution Prevention Programme.
This interactive training programme for community health workers includes:
• Lessons on household energy use and health risks from indoor air pollution.
• Strategies to reduce exposure.
• Practical tools: illustrations, photos, videos, maps and a cost comparison tool for clean energy options.
In 2020, the Kenyan Ministry of Health officially integrated this programme into its national community health worke training curriculum. Since then:
• 2500 community health workers have been trained as trainers.
• The programme is being scaled up nationwide through Kenya’s community health promoters.
• Rwanda and Uganda are now introducing the programme through their ministries of health.
Note: Countries selected are already included in the WHO HEART reports. ## China heating pumps
Since 2015, China's household clean heating policy has scaled up across northern China, banning household coal burning and subsidizing clean heating options (especially electric heaters/heat pumps and electricity).
By 2021, the policy had reached more than 36 million households in northern China.
Field evaluations show measurable health benefits, including reductions in myocardial cardiovascular disease and improvements in blood pressure and respiratory symptoms.
Heating pump devices can “provide heating, cooling and sanitary hot water for residential, commercial and industrial applications. They transform energy from the air, ground and water to useful heat. This transformation is done via the refrigerant cycle”.
Source: European Heat Pump Association.
Policy uptake was high: heat pump/electric heater use increased from about 3% at baseline to above 90% after implementation. The policy increased indoor winter temperature by \~1–2°C and reduced indoor seasonal PM<sub>2.5</sub> by \~20 μg/m<sup>3</sup>.
Health benefits are expected for both women and men; while sex-differentiated effects vary across studies; overall health gains are observed across populations.

Heating pump devices can “provide heating, cooling and sanitary hot water for residential, commercial and industrial applications. They transform energy from the air, ground and water to useful heat. This transformation is done via the refrigerant cycle”.
Due to its intensive industrialization, population density and its long heating season, northern China’s air is one of most polluted in the country. Recently launched, the Clean Heating Plan for northern China in winter for 2017–2021 is a campaign aimed at replacing polluting space heating with solid fuels (largely coal) with electric heat pumps or natural gas. This is being rolled out in Beijing, Tianjin and 26 other municipalities. The reductions in air pollution indoors and outdoors will result in major health benefits through reduction in $\mathsf { P M } _ { 2 . 5 }$ emissions and exposure levels.
Women are those expected to have greater benefits from this campaign as they spend a consistently higher amount of time in the kitchen than men.

# National Efficient Cooking Plan: towards energy sovereignty
• From clean to cleaner intervention.
• 3 million LPG stoves will be replaced with induction stoves.
US\$ 11.6 billion in new hydroelectric power stations and infrastructure (11% of GDP).
More than 80% of electricity generated ted through hydroelectric power stations.
• Climate change mitigation.
A case study from Ecuador.
<drawing id="im-43a95bd10ce7a1c392e48c276a194cc5-0119" format="jpg" path="air-38_WHO_Fact sheet 附件_Clean household energy solutions (清洁家用能源)_2024.blocks.assets/95fbe9851948d31494974b992c31151749db4f5c05f6cb60e4b50763f5b7da24.jpg" src="" />
This is an example of a programme encouraging transition from a clean energy option to an even cleaner one.
Ecuador is indeed working to switch every LPG stove in the country to an induction cooking system based on electricity. The National Ecuadorian Efficient Cooking Plan (NECP) is the first of its kind in the country. The two major highlights goals are:
• Replacing 3 million LPG stoves with induction stoves, covering for 83% of the total population.
• Progress towards energy sovereignty through massive investment in new hydroelectric power stations in the country by 2022, instead of imported LPG which is subsidized by the government (covering 90% of its price).
Although both energy types are considered clean, induction technology is more efficient in terms of time and intensity of cooking.
After the implementation of 3 million induction cook stoves, the programme will continue to replace LPG with induction technology at an annual rate of 30%.
This project is also a climate change mitigation policy action that will help Ecuador become less dependent on fossil fuels, as it replaces LPG with renewable energy (hydroelectric power). The reduction in greenhouse gases emissions from this activity is estimated to be approximately 2.8 million tonnes of $\mathsf { C O } _ { 2 } .$ -equivalent per year.

content:
## A case study from India.
In 2016, the Government of India launched the Pradhan Mantri Ujjwala Yojana (PMUY) – also known as Ujjwala – to provide LPG connections to 5 crore (50 million) women in below the poverty line families over 3 years, starting from 2016. The objective was to provide clean fuel to poor households, especially in rural areas. The government provides a deposit-free LPG connection to the adult woman member of an eligible family and pays for each new connection, while the customer pays for the stove and the first refill. Important aspects of the scheme are: the connection is issued to female members of below the poverty line households who suffer from at least one deprivation, as per the Indian socioeconomic caste census (rural data).
As of late 2023, the programme claims to have connected 99 million households to the LPG system. The scheme was replaced by Ujjwala 2.0 in 2021, which eased some eligibility criteria to ensure that all poor households were eligible for the programme. As of late 2023, 19 million LPG connections have been released under Ujjwala 2.0.
heading: A case study from India.
parent_headings: Pradhan Mantri Ujjwala Yojana LPG programme

content:
## Limitations
While the number of LPG connections grew from 10.2% in 2015–2016 to 16.2% in 2016–2017, there was only a negligible increase in LPG consumption, which rose from 9% in 2015–2016 to 9.8% in 2016–2017. This confirms reports that few PMUY customers buy refills. This is not surprising, as PMUY beneficiaries do not have to pay the security deposit when LPG connections are fitted, and they have the option of paying for a gas stove and the first refill in instalments, while there is no concession for the second refill. Limitations therefore centre around affordability (for refilling cylinders), behavioural aspects and the distribution network, which must be taken into consideration in order for the scheme to be effective in the long run.

## A case study from Nepal.
The Biogas Sector Partnership (BSP) and the National Rural and Renewable Energy Programme, implemented by Alternative Energy Promotion Centre (AEPC), installed more than 432 000 biogas plants across districts in Nepal. Around 100 000 were installed using credit from various commercial banks and microfinancing institutions. AEPC, a governmental agency under the Ministry of Energy, Water Resources and Irrigation, assists in the formulation and implementation of appropriate policies and programmes, resource mobilization, coordination and information management in the renewable energy sector with a focus on energy access in rural areas. BSP subsidizes the upfront installation cost, sets up supply chains and maintenance protocols, supervises the construction and trains household members on how to operate the system safely. The units can last 20 years. Dung and other materials added to the tank and mixed with water every day are free, and so is the gas that comes out of the pipe. The fuel savings from avoided LPG, wood and kerosene usage exceed the cost of the system within 3 years. The BSP is a model ripe for replication and scaling up in other settings, especially rural areas where people rely on polluting fuels and technologies for cooking, and where keeping livestock is common.
BSP is a government-initiated programme to promote biogas plants for cooking and lighting in the country mostly using cow dung. The concept was tested in the 1980s and then expanded by BSP in the 1990s with the aims of reducing deforestation, improving indoor air quality and providing a renewable energy source for rural households.

## A case study from Rwanda.
The aim of the Rwanda Energy Access and Quality Improvement Project is to increase access to clean cooking solutions for 500 000 Rwandan households.
Component b of the project established a “clean cooking results-based financing” scheme – a partial subsidy for the purchase of clean, efficient cooking solutions by eligible households to improve the affordability of clean cooking technologies. Socioeconomic ubudehe (local collective) levels 1, 2 and 3 are eligible for the programme reducing prices for the lowest income populations in Rwanda.
The subsidy is co-financed by the World Bank’s Clean Cooking Fund. The aim is to provide access to clean cooking technologies to at least 500 000 households, of which 25% are to be headed by a woman, comprising 2.15 million Rwandans. The subsidy is also designed to decrease the dependence of urban populations on wood for fuel. The project aims to attract private sector financing, build more partnerships and engage other stakeholders in promoting green investments for clean cooking.
On 4 November 2021, Rwanda and Sustainable Energy for All launched the Energy Compact on Clean Cooking. The compact is a crucial step in transforming the country’s energy use towards a greener, more sustainable future by reducing the proportion of households using wood for cooking from 79.9% in 2017 to 42% by 2024. This subsidy scheme is conducted in a partnership with the Rwanda Development Bank and the Energy Development Corporation.

## Glossary
Biogas: A methane-rich gas produced through the anaerobic (without air) digestion of organic wastes. It can be generated from animal and kitchen wastes, as well as some crop residues.
Ethanol/alcohol: Clean liquid biofuel that can be made from a variety of feedstocks, including sugary materials such as sugar cane, molasses, sugar beet or sweet sorghum; starchy materials such as cassava (manioc), potatoes or maize; or cellulosic materials such as wood, grasses, corn stover and other agricultural residues.
Fuel stacking: Fuel stacking is the parallel use of multiple types of fuel and technologies in a single household.
Household air pollution: Air pollution generated by household fuel combustion, leading to indoor air pollution and contributing to ambient air pollution.
Liquefied petroleum gas: Co-product of natural gas and crude oil production and usually consists of a mixture of propane and butane for standard heating and cooking purposes.
Off-grid: Not using or depending on public utilities, especially electricity supply.
Products of incomplete combustion: Mixtures of pollutant particles and gases formed by incomplete burning of fuel or other material.
Solar: Direct sunlight is used to heat and cook by directing the sun’s thermal energy to power solar cook stoves.
